brief.head: Rewired by the map
brief.text: What we engage with, book or phone, changes the brain itself, Amit Varma said. London’s taxi drivers had their brains rewired once they relied on maps. {#taxi}

brief.head: Ten-letter words
brief.text: Children who hear ten-letter words from birth to five, Varma said, citing Jim Heckman, gain a layer of intelligence that cannot be made up later. {120-R06}

brief.head: This too shall pass
brief.text: In the concentration camps, Viktor Frankl wrote, literature gave inmates solace. It tells us, Varma said, that we are not alone, and that this too shall pass. {120-C04}

brief.text: Ajay Shah’s backpack holds a laptop full of distractions and an iPad with none. The iPad is an old one, with only a book reader and a throwaway account. {#ipad}

brief.head: Go down rabbit holes
brief.text: When a subject grabs you, Varma said, chase the footnotes, ask ChatGPT, check Wikipedia and buy the next book. “Do not think of these as digressions.” {120-C13}

thought.text: Reading is actually what can save solitude from loneliness.
thought.who: Amit Varma, giving his ninth reason to read, with Schopenhauer and Harold Bloom in support

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why, and how, to read
lead.head: Booked for life
body: Amit Varma opened with a lesson in close reading. To be a huge fan of hoodies, he explained, is to be huge, and a fan of hoodies. “A careful reading will reward you with additional meaning and layers.” {120-J01}

The rest of the episode was a primer in three parts: why to read, how to build the habit, and how to read a book. Ajay Shah played the busy sceptic, too occupied scrolling Instagram to read. Varma promised that within minutes Shah would delete the app and become a dedicated reader.
## The case for books
Varma offered eleven reasons to read. The number was no risk, he said, “because Ajay can’t count, but Amit can.”

The first was that reading supplies the dots we connect to picture the world. Experience shows only the present, and a narrow slice of it. “The more dots we have, the more high definition our picture,” he said. {120-C01}
Shah put it another way. A practical person reaches seventy with the knowledge of one life. A reader taps the knowledge of hundreds or thousands.

Reading, Varma went on, is good for the brain, the heart and the psyche. It makes better citizens and more creative writers, carries a conversation across time and builds a latticework of mental models. It saves solitude from loneliness, gives joy, and helps you know yourself.
Shah added a caution: reading does not guarantee goodness. Joseph Stalin, he said, was very well read.
## The habit
Wanting to read is the easy part. “I think the key word here which I want to emphasise is habit,” Varma said.

Start small, he advised, read often rather than long, tie reading to an existing routine, keep books within reach and find fellow readers. Above all, begin with identity: if the best version of you is a reader, be that person. {120-C10}
## Reading the book

For nonfiction, Varma turned to Mortimer Adler’s four levels of reading, which run from making sense of sentences to reading many books on a single subject. {120-R01} For fiction, he followed Harold Bloom: slow down, and never skim.
He ended with four closing thoughts. Format doesn’t matter. It is fine to quit a book. Reading is not a competition. And identity comes first.
On quitting, he offered a sum. An optimistic life expectancy, times an optimistic number of books a year, gives the most you will ever read: a pitiful fraction of all that exists.
Shah, by his own account “the world’s slowest reader”, reads pages slowly but deeply. Reading well, he argued, is like eating well: easier as a household than alone.
Both hosts bristled at AI summaries of books. “Books are not information,” Shah said. {120-C19} What matters, he said, is the ten or twenty hours of intimate conversation with one great author.
Varma closed by showing how he takes notes on a book, chapter by chapter and theme by theme, in an app called Roam Research.

second.label: Reading and goodness
second.head: Marginalia of a monster
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why reading is no guarantee of goodness
body: By reading, Ajay Shah said, we impose a positive externality on the world, making those around us think and debate better. {120-C06} But reading is not a sufficient condition for goodness.

His exhibit was Joseph Stalin, whom he ranked history’s second-worst monster, after Chairman Mao and ahead of Hitler. {120-S03} Citing, he thought, Stephen Kotkin, Shah said Stalin could have held an hour’s comfortable conversation with any philosopher. He read intensively and scribbled in his books.

Amit Varma added Mao, a foundational thinker on guerrilla warfare; Shah stressed that Mao had theorised his way there. That, Varma said, was like Shah theorising about the world and then doing a YouTube show. “Those who can do,” Shah replied, “the others become podcasters.” {120-J03}

quote.text: He was considered an extremely sophisticated and erudite person. He was very well read.

second.caption: Stalin the reader

third.head: Summary judgment
body: On a drive in DC last year, a friend proudly told Amit Varma that he had AI make 500-word summaries of Varma’s eight-hour episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen*. {120-S11} He expected approval, and did the same with books.

“I was literally viscerally angry, not because it’s my show,” Varma said, “but because that’s such a stupid way of consuming knowledge.” A book, he said, teaches you how to think, and there is no shortcut for that.

Ajay Shah, citing a New York Times podcast conversation by Ezra Klein, had noted that a thousand-word summary can make you look sophisticated at a cocktail party. {#cocktail} We read, he said, for the hours of intimate conversation with the author.
“Books are not information,” Shah said. “Information is trivial. You can look it up.” {120-C19}

p2.title: A primer on reading
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s guide in three parts: why read, how to build the habit, how to read a book

sections.label: Part One
sections.head: Eleven reasons to open a book
sections.caption: eleven reasons to read
body: Amit Varma gave eleven reasons to read, and the first was about dots. We paint pictures of the world by connecting them, he said, and the more we have, the sharper the picture. {120-C01}

Experience alone cannot supply them. A friend who knew Narendra Modi told Varma how Modi once wept recalling a childhood night when his mother was ill and hot, and he flicked the fan switch to find no electricity. Modi grasped power and roads because he had lived them, Varma said. But spontaneous order cannot be seen with your own eyes. {120-S02}
Ajay Shah put it in lives: a practical doer reaches seventy with one life’s knowledge, a reader with that of thousands.
## Brain, heart and psyche

Reading is good for the brain, Varma said: scrolling hops from factoid to factoid, while books build connections. It is good for the heart, because reading expands what Martha Nussbaum calls narrative imagination. {120-C03}
Shah recalled reading that Tolstoy, writing *War and Peace*, walked around his house sobbing uncontrollably, lost in the minds of his characters. {120-S04}

Reading also makes for informed citizens, feeds creativity and carries a conversation across time. It builds what Charlie Munger called a latticework of models, which, Varma said, is where the show gets its name. {120-C09}
~ And it saves solitude from loneliness, brings joy and helps you know yourself.

quote.text: George Eliot called reading the nearest thing to life.

sections.label: Part Two
sections.head: Identity first, pages second
sections.caption: building a reading habit
body: The key word, Amit Varma said, is habit. Don’t set yourself a target, such as finishing a prize-winner. James Clear, in *Atomic Habits*, calls habits the compound interest of self-improvement.
Be bloody-minded for at least three months, Varma advised, until the loop is hardwired in the basal ganglia and reading feels automatic. {#threemonths}

Better still, start from identity. Ask who the best version of you is. If that person reaches for a book instead of a phone, actions flow from the self-image, and a missed day does not break you. {120-C10}
## Small, often, anchored
Start small, with two pages or fifteen minutes. “Frequency matters more than duration,” Varma said, and Ajay Shah laughed. {120-J08}

Anchor reading to a routine such as morning coffee or the commute, because neurons that fire together wire together. Keep books everywhere, put the Kindle app up front and take the social media apps out. {#kindle}

~ Decide in advance what to read next, to spare yourself decision fatigue. Reward yourself, as James Clear’s writer did by moving a hairpin between jars for every paragraph. {120-R10} And find a community of readers.

quote.text: But my slogan for you would be just be it.

sections.label: Part Three
sections.head: Tasted, swallowed, chewed
sections.caption: how to read a book
body: Amit Varma drew his guide to the act of reading from three books, beginning with Mortimer Adler’s *How to Read a Book* and its four levels of reading. {120-R01}

Elementary reading is making sense of sentences. Inspectional reading is a first date with the book: the contents, the preface, a skim to see whether it is really an essay padded out, as many nonfiction books are. Francis Fukuyama’s *The End of History and the Last Man*, Varma said, is a rare book that goes well beyond its essay. {120-R13}

Analytical reading means chewing: classify the book, state its gist, outline its parts and name the problem the author is trying to solve. Synoptical reading means many books on one subject; Varma read some thirty for two episodes on Gandhi. {120-S08}
## Slow down for stories

Fiction, Varma said, following Harold Bloom’s *How to Read and Why*, should never be skimmed. Short stories favour the tacit and make the reader discern what the writer leaves out. Memorise poems. {120-C14} Read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.
~ Francine Prose’s *Reading Like a Writer* adds an eye for the author’s tools, from the clipped sentences of hard-boiled crime fiction to Saramago’s pages-long ones.

quote.text: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.
quote.who: Francis Bacon, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Closing thoughts
sections.head: Drop the book, not the habit
sections.caption: quitting books, and other closing thoughts
body: Format doesn’t matter, Amit Varma said. “Literature is words. That’s what they are. Everything else is packaging.” Insisting on physical books shows nostalgia, not love of literature. {120-C15}
Audiobooks are a somewhat different experience, since you cannot easily stop and reread. But they let someone hanging on a local train spend that half-hour with words.
## A lifetime budget

It is fine to quit a book. Multiply an optimistic life expectancy by an optimistic number of books a year, and the answer is pitifully small beside the millions written. “Don’t throw good time after bad,” he said. {120-C16}
Don’t feel guilty about abandoning a prize-winner everyone loves, and don’t be a snob: an airport bestseller or an academic paper is fine if it brings enjoyment or enlightenment.
Nor is reading a competition. Varma once said, quite honestly, that he had read two hundred books in a year, and was abused on Twitter for showing off. He has not mentioned a number since. {120-S09}
~ His speed, he said, comes from a habit begun at three or four. What matters is the time spent in a contemplative state, not the score.

quote.text: There is no Olympics of reading.

sections.label: Ajay’s additions
sections.head: Slow and deep, and together
sections.caption: reading slowly, and reading together
body: Ajay Shah had a confession. He reads with only one mode, slowly, playing with every sentence, word and argument. He would like to read three times the papers and ten times the books he does. {120-S10}
He has stopped fighting it. Everything that has happened to him, he said, has come out of reading this way, though he is not saying it is good for everyone.
## A household of readers

His second point was about food. In a household where junk food is bought and white rice comes out of the kitchen, eating healthy takes a superhuman effort, so modern thinking on nutrition changes the whole food environment. Reading well, like eating well, is harder alone. {120-C18}
Viewers have told him the best way to watch the show is in a group that hits pause at every chapter break to argue. {#groupview} That turns passive consumption into active learning.
Amit Varma wondered what such groups might be saying. Perhaps: “How would the show look with two Ajays talking to each other?” {120-J14}
~ When three people in the room disagree and talk it out, Shah said, the knowledge becomes their own.

quote.text: I’m the world’s slowest reader. I read pages slowly, but I read them deeply.

sections.label: Amit’s method
sections.head: Mapping the territory
sections.caption: taking notes in Roam Research
body: Amit Varma closed with a demonstration of how he takes notes on a book in Roam Research, an app he loves for its nested entries and bidirectional links.

Reading Ghazala Wahab’s *Born a Muslim* for an episode, he first set down the chapter titles as top-level entries, then nested every point beneath them and every quote a level deeper. One was a beautiful example of show, don’t tell: a grandfather who, in winter, shelled pine nuts during the day to reward the children in the evening. {#pinenuts}
Earlier, he said, he kept sixty pages of Microsoft Word and scrolled frantically. {120-C20} Now any term in double brackets becomes a link that gathers every related quote.
## A layer of themes

When material has no chapters, he builds a structure of his own. Mahima Vashisht, one of his writing students, had written more than a hundred posts of her newsletter, *Womaning in India*. {#hundredposts}
Varma listed the posts, then opened a section called themes: controlling female sexuality, stereotypes, a world designed by men, for men. That let him approach her material thematically.
~ The method works even without a podcast to prepare, he said. “Now I understand the territory.”

quote.text: No, bro. I’m kind of reading them out from this.

side.boxText: *How to Read a Book* by Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren sets out four levels of reading, and a four-step method for chewing a book: classify it, state its gist, outline its parts, name its problem. {120-R01}

contQuote.text: We read books because for that duration of ten hours or twenty hours, we are with the author in an intimate conversation. We are grappling with the argument, we are grappling with complex ideas.

p3.title: Tales from the shelf
p3.deck: A snooze skipped, a father’s gift, a jar of paperclips and a poker face

stories.start: So I gotta tell you something. We are in um this place
stories.end: when you discover something that has that effect in you, you should embrace it
stories.caption: the book that beat his snooze button
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the book he found by accident
stories.head: Searched for Bloom, found Virtue
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah shoot about six episodes in three days, and this was the sixth. The night before, Varma went to bed super tired and super stressed about the prep still to be done.

Before sleeping, he switched on his iPad and searched his Kindle for “Bloom”, meaning only to keep Harold Bloom’s book ready, not even to read it. The search also turned up books published by Bloomsbury. {#bloomsbury}

One was Alasdair MacIntyre’s *After Virtue*. Suyash Rai, a dear friend of the hosts and, Varma said, a great thinker, had recommended it a long time ago; MacIntyre is a great influence on him. Varma bought the book immediately, and then did not read it.

A few weeks earlier, Pratap Bhanu Mehta had taken him to lunch in Bombay and spoken of MacIntyre, who had died in May. That was another prick in his head: “dude, what are you doing? You gotta read this guy.”
That night he read the first chapter and half of the second before sleep won. He woke with the argument running through his head.
“I typically will hit Snooze 17 times before I get up,” he said. “But I kinda jumped out of bed because I was like, I have to read the book.” {120-S05}
~ Later, over coffee at the dining table, he read on instead of prepping for this episode. He had to know how the chapter finished.
stories.why: Serendipity and pleasure, not duty, drive a reading life. Ideas books, Varma said, can expand the brain and grip you as hard as stories do. When one has that effect on you, embrace it.
stories.postscript: Varma had gone looking for Harold Bloom’s *How to Read and Why*, which he went on to recommend in the episode. {120-R02}

stories.start: my father had the sixty volume collection of great books of the Western world
stories.end: And then I just have to go to that volume and read Nietzsche
stories.caption: his father’s Great Books
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his father’s sixty volumes
stories.head: Great Books, kept for a father
body: Amit Varma’s father owned the sixty-volume *Great Books of the Western World*. For about ten years before he died, he kept telling his son to take it to Bombay: “This is for you. I really want you to have this.”
Varma kept refusing. “In Bombay, the cost of a book is not what you pay for it, but the real estate it occupies,” he said. His little rented house had no space. {120-S07}
After his father died, his library of many thousands of books went to a community library. Varma kept the sixty, as a memory of his dad.

~ The two he does read sit on his desk: the Synopticon, Mortimer Adler’s essays on themes like love, death and desire across the whole canon. “It fills me with such awe, it fills me with such joy.” {#awe}
stories.why: Books can be kept out of love rather than use. The Synopticon also shows synoptical reading at work: one quote, Varma said, can send him straight to another author’s volume, as when he found a line from Nietzsche.

stories.start: So there was a point at which at NIPFP Ila Patnaik was irritated
stories.end: So the flow of Rubbish interrupts that were coming to her went down dramatically
stories.caption: Ila Patnaik’s paperclip jar
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a colleague’s cure for constant interruptions
stories.head: The price of a question
body: At NIPFP, Ila Patnaik was irritated that the admin team kept coming to her for decisions it could make itself. Her view, as Ajay Shah put it: “I have no great value added in what needs to be done, you figure it out.”
Her solution was a jar. “Each time you come to me to ask me a question, you have to put one paper clip into this jar,” Shah said. “It worked dramatically.” {120-S06}
People would put in a paperclip, hang their heads in shame, and then ask. The flow of rubbish interruptions fell dramatically, and the team became more thoughtful.
~ Amit Varma recalled the famous thought experiment in AI about a paperclip maximiser. “It turns out that Ila is a paperclip minimiser,” he said. {120-J11}
stories.why: A tiny, visible cost can change behaviour more than a lecture. It makes people pause and ask whether a question is really worth asking: gamification, run in reverse. Ajay Shah told it as a trick for building habits.

stories.start: I became a fan of hoodies when I was a professional poker player
stories.end: So anyway, so that is my love for the hoodie.
stories.caption: poker tells and hoodies
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on tells, smiles and hiding his face
stories.head: Poker face, under a hood
body: Amit Varma became a fan of hoodies when he was a professional poker player, between 2010 and 2015. {#poker} Poker is fundamentally maths, he said, but in live games you can give away tells.
So after betting he would cover his face, avoid eye contact, look at the table and keep everything exactly the same, bluffing or not. Opponents watch for dilating pupils or a pulsing carotid artery.

His own favourite tell was a joke. “Human beings have two kinds of smiles,” he said. “There’s a fake smile and a genuine smile.” A genuine smile means a player is comfortable; a fake one means he is worried. {120-S01}
~ Even then, Varma said, you only update your priors a little. The man with the fake smile might just have a great hand, and an urgent need for the loo.
stories.why: Since signals leak, the disciplined player shuts the channel entirely, showing the same blank posture every time. And no tell, however reliable, settles anything: it only nudges a judgement that remains uncertain.
stories.postscript: He opened by parsing his own sentence: being “a huge fan of hoodies” means he is huge, and a fan of hoodies. {120-J01}

quiz.q: Which four levels of reading does Mortimer Adler describe in *How to Read a Book*?
quiz.a: Elementary, inspectional, analytical and synoptical: from sentences to many books on one subject.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma refuse, for about ten years, to take his father’s sixty volumes to Bombay?
quiz.a: In Bombay, a book’s real cost is the real estate it occupies.

quiz.q: What did Ila Patnaik make her admin team do before asking her a question?
quiz.a: Drop a paperclip into a jar, which cut trivial interruptions dramatically.

quiz.q: What does Harold Bloom, as Amit Varma reported, advise readers to do with poems?
quiz.a: Memorise them, so the poem possesses you and you can read it more closely.

quiz.q: How does Amit Varma work out your lifetime book budget, and what follows from it?
quiz.a: Multiply optimistic life expectancy by books a year; the total is small, so quit freely.

quiz.q: According to Amit Varma, where does the show’s name, *Everything is Everything*, come from?
quiz.a: Reading reveals the interconnectedness of everything, even fields of study kept in separate silos.
